title: Figure 9.1 looks confusing
description:
Figure 9.1 and the relating descriptions seem to claim that minimizing RMSE and maximizing coefficient of determination (R-squared) are different and lead to different predictions, which is confusing to me. 
I suppose R-squared is defined as $R^2 = 1 – \frac{\Sigma_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y_i})^2}{\Sigma_{i=1}^{n}{(y_i – \bar{y})^2}}$ and that reduces to $R^2 = 1 – \frac{n \cdot {RMSE}^2}{\Sigma_{i=1}^{n}{(y_i – \bar{y})^2}}$.
Because $y_i$ and $\bar{y}$ do not change for the same dataset, minimizing RMSE should be equivalent to maximizing $R^2$.
Have I misunderstood anything...? (maybe coefficient of determination defined differently?) 

And I suppose RMSE and MAE (Mean Absolute Error) would be one of the candidates of sets of metrics that would clearly lead to different predictions.
Thank you for the great guide anyways.

title: Positional arguments in examples
description:
This is more of a personal preference rather than an actual issue, but I think it could help users understand the code examples better.

The book (which is great by the way) seems to use a lot of arbitrary positional arguments in function calls mixed with keyword arguments. In general I really dislike using positional arguments: I find the code harder to read and interpret, particularly if you are not super familiar with the functions in question. Here is a simple example from Ch. 11.

```lm_models <- 
  lm_models %>% 
  workflow_map("fit_resamples", 
               # Options to `workflow_map()`: 
               seed = 1101, verbose = TRUE,
               # Options to `fit_resamples()`: 
               resamples = ames_folds, control = keep_pred)
#> i 1 of 3 resampling: basic_lm
#> ✔ 1 of 3 resampling: basic_lm (2.9s)
#> i 2 of 3 resampling: interact_lm
#> ✔ 2 of 3 resampling: interact_lm (3s)
#> i 3 of 3 resampling: splines_lm
#> ✔ 3 of 3 resampling: splines_lm (4.4s)
```

Looking at this function, it is not immediately obvious what `"fit_resamples"` is. Copying the code into RStudio means you can quickly see the function documentation to find out what the arguments are, but looking at the text gives no indication of what it is. There are many more examples throughout the book.

Seeing the argument name makes it easier to understand how the function works, for me at least. I feel it would be helpful to use named arguments wherever possible, particularly when using functions for the first time.

title: Suggestion to improve code in TMwR where parallel processing is involved
description:
I was trying to knit the gitbook version of the book TMwR, but I was unable to. I am using a Windows system, and doMC package doesn't work on it. In the later chapters (like Chapter 15 of workflow-sets) there is a code so that it can work on both, Windows and non-Windows system. However, this code, which involves using grepl function and R.Version()$platform to decide whether this system has Windows or any other operating system, it was not working on my laptop. 
When I write in console `R.Version()$platform`, the output is `"x86_64-w64-mingw32"`. So, I changed the code as follows:

```
cores <- parallel::detectCores()
if(Sys.info()['sysname']=="Windows"){
   library(doParallel)
   cl <- makePSOCKcluster(cores)
   registerDoParallel(cl)
}else {
   library(doMC)
   registerDoMC(cores = cores)
}
```
After this change, the code is working now.

title: Suggestion: Mention the controversial nature of subsampling

Section 8.4.5 mentions that subsampling (e.g., oversampling, undersampling, and hybrid) approaches "can be used to address class imbalance via subsampling". - Pozzolo, A. D., Caelen, O., Johnson, R. A. & Bontempi, G. Calibrating probability with undersampling for unbalanced classification. In IEEE Symposium Series on Computational Intelligence, SSCI 2015, Cape Town, South Africa, December 7–10, 2015 159–166 (IEEE, 2015).

title: Suggestion: Consider replacing interaction example
description:
Section 8.4.2 provides the following example of a possible interaction effect:

> For example, if you were trying to predict your morning commute time, two potential predictors could be the amount of traffic and the time of day. However, the relationship between commute time and the amount of traffic is different for different times of day.

I think this example may be confusing to some readers because it is hard to imagine what effect time of day could have on commute time that does not operate through the amount of traffic. title: Error with end-of-chapter references
description:
The current citation style uses "---" rather than repeating authors on subsequent lines, e.g.,
>  Bradley, R, and M Terry. 1952. “Rank Analysis of Incomplete Block Designs: I. The Method of Paired Comparisons.” Biometrika 39 (3/4): 324–45.
> Breiman, L. 1996a. “Bagging Predictors.” Machine Learning 24 (2): 123–40.
> ———. 1996b. “Stacked Regressions.” Machine Learning 24 (1): 49–64. 

This works great in the references chapter at the end of the book where all references are present. However, it leads to problems in the end-of-chapter reference sections where "---" is used out of context, e.g.,


> ———. 2001a. “Random Forests.” Machine Learning 45 (1): 5–32.
> Davison, A, and D Hinkley. 1997. Bootstrap Methods and Their Application. Vol. 1. Cambridge university press.
> Hyndman, R, and G Athanasopoulos. 2018. Forecasting: Principles and Practice. OTexts.
> ———. 2020. Feature Engineering and Selection: A Practical Approach for Predictive Models. CRC Press.
> Schmidberger, M, M Morgan, D Eddelbuettel, H Yu, L Tierney, and U Mansmann. 2009. “State of the Art in Parallel Computing with R.” Journal of Statistical Software 31 (1): 1–27. https://www.jstatsoft.org/v031/i01.
> Xu, Q, and Y Liang. 2001. “Monte Carlo Cross Validation.” Chemometrics and Intelligent Laboratory Systems 56 (1): 1–11.

I recommend either rendering the citations per chapter separately (if possible) or choosing a different citation style that makes the authors explicit (even when repeated).

title: Both the guidebook and Julia Silge's videos on glmnet lack a method for (creating a new column of) predicted values using elastic net
description:
References (same page, different sections): https://www.tmwr.org/models.html#create-a-model and https://www.tmwr.org/models.html#use-the-model-results

In situations when elastic net or `glmnet` is used instead of linear regression, this guide doesn't really work. Here is what the guide says (copy/pasted):
```
lm_form_fit
#> parsnip model object
#> 
#> Fit time:  4ms 
#> 
#> Call:
#> stats::lm(formula = Sale_Price ~ Longitude + Latitude, data = data)
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#> (Intercept)    Longitude     Latitude  
#>     -300.25        -2.01         2.78
```
When in fact, `glmnet` output will look something more like this:
```
Call:  glmnet::glmnet(x = maybe_matrix(x), y = y, family = "gaussian",      alpha = ~0.5) 

   Df  %Dev Lambda
1   0  0.00 727400
2   1  0.99 662800
3   2  1.88 603900
4   2  2.68 550300
5   2  3.36 501400
6   2  3.94 456900
...
```
where generally, it would be more than 50 more rows of output. For elastic net from `glmnet`, what the guide's code needs is `tidy()`, taken from Julia Silge's video [here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R32AsuKICAY).

However, using `predict()` for `glmnet` throws the error:
```
Error in predict.glmnet(spec_enet1_fit, new_data = df_test_small) : 
You need to supply a value for 'newx'
```

Both the guidebook and Julia Silge's video lack a method for creating a new column of predicted values using elastic net, as well as creating a graph for them (though I think that's going to be a lot easier).

## The problem

The tutorial code in Ch. 15 is returning errors that prevent readers from viewing the tuning results:
```
Error: Some elements of 'result' do not have class `tune_results`.
```
Perhaps these errors are related to `tune` and `workflowsets`?

In addition to creating a reprex below (that uses the default supplied data), I've ran the same code on my own project data and the errors persist. Since the error comes up as `SVM_radial` tunes, I also tried running the code with all of the models listed in the `normalized` workflow set removed, to no avail.

Lastly, the following warnings when tuning the `xgboost` model in the tutorial seem a bit strange:
```
A correlation computation is required, but `estimate` is constant and has 0 standard deviation, resulting in a divide by 0 error. `NA` will be returned.
```
The warnings are mentioned in tidymodels/tune#37 and tidymodels/tune#116. I don't quite understand these warnings because I've successfully tuned my own `xgboost` models on similar data without encountering them. Would they be suppressed if `rsq` wasn't calculated?

- This discussion currently is located in the section "Using a recipe with traditional modeling functions" but I'd like to suggest moving this since it isn't related to using a base R or non-tidymodels model. > There are a few existing R packages that provide a unified interface to harmonize these heterogeneous modeling APIs, such as `caret` and `mlr`. tidymodels takes a similar approach to unification of the function interface as well as enforcing consistency in the function names and return values.

title: Fig 1.3: modeling schematic
description:
My perspective is that most folks will be a little puzzled about a few characteristics of the modeling schematic, specifically what the difference is between EDA and quantitative analysis and where model evaluation takes place. I'd like for us to change up this plot.

- On the first point, I have heard the term ["EDA"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exploratory_data_analysis) to be typically used to mean to include visual methods but not to be solely visual methods. I don't think we should break out something like quantitative analysis separately from EDA because people mean those quantitative, numerical "side quests" when they say EDA.

- I think we should either add some bars for model evaluation (like after Model 4, the second Model 2, the second Model 4) or discuss in words where we picture this happening, or what task it is a subtask of.

title: Confusing box-text and example pair in fit (7.2 / 7.3)
description:
The book seems well written and concise. While going through it I stumbled over a slightly confusing section with Fit however.  
For references I am reading the current (as of 2020-09-18) version of the book [online](https://www.tmwr.org/models.html). 

In a box in section 7.2 (Use the model results) there is a box stating
> Never pass the fit element of a parsnip model to a model prediction function; see Section 7.3 for making predictions. If the data were preprocessed in any way, incorrect predictions will be generated (sometimes, without errors). The underlying model’s prediction function has no idea if any transformations have been made to the data prior to running the model.

and then following the link for section 7.3 the example shows (quite correctly) that one simply uses `predict` to make predictions, with a slightly altered syntax (new_data rather than newdata). For new (and even experienced) users of R, which might not be used to using `S3` functions directly (eg. `predict.lm`). 

It feels like the distinction isn't immediately clear, and that it could be made clear by adding a small example such as in the example below:
> Never pass the fit element of a parsnip model to a model prediction function (for example `predict.lm` for models fit using `lm`); see Section 7.3 for making predictions. If the data were preprocessed in any way, incorrect predictions will be generated (sometimes, without errors). The underlying model’s prediction function has no idea if any transformations have been made to the data prior to running the model.

title: Latex compilation errors and fixes
description:
There were numerous latex compilation errors when trying to compile to PDF with "bookdown::render_book("index.Rmd", "bookdown::pdf_book")". Specifically:

- Two instances of unescape underscores. Both fixed by changing `kable(escape = FALSE)` to `kable(escape = TRUE)`. 
  - 10-resampling.Rmd: 120
  - pre-proc-table.Rmd: 70
- `Package amsmath error: Erroneous nesting of equation structures;` caused by nesting an `{align}` environment inside an equation ( because $$...$$ compiles to \\[...\\]) in 11-comparing-models.Rmd: 230. I fixed this by removing the $$ tags, but this may break the HTML compilation so may not be a general solution.
- key `pvalue` multiply defined in bibliography. Fixed by removing entry at TMwR.bib: 329

Please note also that the table in pre-proc-table.Rmd overflows the PDF page, likely due to the manually inserted HTML \<tt\> tags. However this does not prevent compilation.

I would have included these as a pull request, but I haven't actually read the book yet so I'm not confident in my RMarkdown coding.
